name: Potentiality and Actuality
plain_explanation: A block of marble is only a 'potential' statue -- it could become one, but is not yet one; once it has been given the sculptor's form, it has become 'actual.' Aristotle uses this potential/actual distinction to describe all change as a movement from less to more form.
precise_definition: Bare matter is conceived as pure potentiality of form; change is the process by which potentiality is realized as actuality; that which has more form is more 'actual,' and God, having no matter, is pure actuality with no potentiality and therefore no possibility of change.
why_it_mattered: It underlies Aristotle's optimistic, teleological view that the universe develops toward ever more organized, actualized (and hence more divine) states.
historical_origin: Developed by Aristotle as the dynamic complement to the matter-form distinction.
examples: 'A block of marble is a potential statue,' meaning 'from a block of marble, by suitable acts, a statue is produced'
objections: Russell argues potentiality is a convenient shorthand only if it can be translated away into statements where it does not appear; used as a fundamental, irreducible concept, it 'always conceals confusion of thought,' and Aristotle's use of it is 'one of the bad points in his system'
